paper.citation: Farley T, Barry E, Sylvester R, De Medici A, Wilson MG. Poor isometric neck extension strength as a risk factor for concussion in male professional Rugby Union players. Br J Sports Med. 2022;0:1-7.
paper.abstract: A prospective cohort of 225 male professional rugby players from 10 Georgian clubs had isometric neck strength measured at preseason, mid-season and end of season, with concussions and match exposure recorded across the season. Each 10% higher neck extension strength was associated with a 13% lower concussion rate (adjusted IRR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.98), and no other strength range or composite was significantly associated.
paper.tldr: In 225 male professional rugby players, weaker isometric neck extension was associated with a higher concussion rate: each 10% increase was linked to a 13% lower rate, though this is an observational association.
paper.methods: Neck strength was tested with a hand-held dynamometer in six ranges at three time points during one season. Concussions were clinically diagnosed by team doctors, match exposure was recorded, and concussion rates were modelled with Poisson regression adjusted for age, club and BMI.
paper.findings: Thirty concussions occurred in 29 players, a rate of 13.7 per 1000 hours played. Extension strength was the only range significantly associated with concussion (adjusted IRR 0.87, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.98, p=0.019). An extension strength of 41 kg or below identified 71% of players who were later concussed, with a 46% false-positive rate, although the Discussion quotes 68%.
paper.limitations: The cohort is observational, so the association does not show that stronger neck extension causes a lower concussion risk. Only 29 players were concussed, end-of-season testing was incomplete (74 of 225 players), and the 41 kg threshold was derived from the same sample with a high false-positive rate. Results come from one league and male professionals only.
paper.practicalImplications: Neck extension strength is a modifiable factor that may be worth including in preseason conditioning for male professional rugby players. The study does not show that neck strengthening reduces concussion, so the strength measure should be treated as a risk marker rather than a proven intervention target.
paper.athleteDev: The findings support including neck extension strength in preseason strength and conditioning for male professional rugby players, with 41 kg as a rough reference point. Because the threshold has a high false-positive rate, it should not be used as a standalone screening cut-off.
paper.rtp: The study addresses concussion incidence, not return to sport after concussion. It cannot be used to set return-to-play criteria or neck strength targets for players recovering from a concussion.
